[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday/visual reading: indentation or line position tells you what belongs together, as in an outline. Java rule: only braces delimit a block; indentation is ignored, and without braces an if or loop body is just the next single statement.
[1] misconception (M) -> LocalVarOutsideScope: wrong rule: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global. Right rule: A local variable's scope runs from its declaration to the end of the enclosing block.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> LocalVarOutsideScope: Applies the block rule (LT: all statements of the block in order, the whole block as one unit) unevenly: includes the statement after the closing brace in the body on one pass but not another, or runs only part of the body. (here mixing in: "A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global")
[3] misconception (M) -> StatementAfterIfInBranch: wrong rule: A statement placed after the if statement belongs to its branch, so it runs only when the condition is true. Right rule: The branch ends at its closing brace (or after its single statement); the next statement runs whatever the condition was.
[4] misconception (M) -> LoopBodyStatementOutsideLoop: wrong rule: Some statements inside the loop braces are not repeated; they run once, before or after the loop. Right rule: Every statement inside the loop braces is part of the body and runs on every pass.
[5] misconception (M) -> StatementAfterLoopInBody: wrong rule: A statement written after the loop is repeated with the loop body. Right rule: The body ends at the closing brace (or after its single statement); code after it runs once, after the loop ends.

[0] names_the_element (N): A block (statement block) is a sequence of statements enclosed in braces { }; it counts as one statement where a single statement is expected.
[1] states_the_rule (S): A block is a sequence of statements and local variable declarations within braces; a variable declared in a block is in scope only from its declaration to the end of that block.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): A block executes each of its statements in order from first to last; if a statement completes abruptly, the rest of the block is skipped.
[1] output_prediction (OP): A block has no value; its result is the combined effect of its statements, in order.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): Entering a block makes room for its local variables; leaving it (at the closing brace) ends their scope, so they can no longer be used.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): A block is built from statements, each ended by ;, and is itself usable as a single statement (e.g. a loop body).
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Indentation should show block nesting, but only braces define it; layout that disagrees with the braces misleads the reader, not the compiler.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Purpose: group several statements so they act as one body (of main, an if branch or a loop) and limit the scope of variables to where they are needed.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> LocalVarOutsideScope: Adding braces around a single-statement body keeps behaviour; adding a second statement to a braceless body changes it (the new statement runs outside); moving a declaration into a block makes later uses outside the block fail to compile.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Every { must be matched by a }. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: a missing or extra brace: javac reports '{' expected, 'class' or 'interface' expected, or reached end of file while parsing, often on a later line
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use a block whenever a body has more than one statement (S&W and TJ advise braces even for one), and declare variables in the innermost block that needs them.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Without braces only one statement is the body. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: a multi-statement body written without braces, indented as if all were inside
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A local variable is visible only inside its block. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: using a variable after the block that declared it has closed (cannot find symbol)

wrong: Indents nested blocks inconsistently, so the visual nesting differs from the real nesting. | right: Indent consistently, one level deeper for each nested block, so the layout shows the real nesting; the compiler ignores indentation.
wrong: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global. | right: A local variable exists only from its declaration to the end of its block.

wrong: Some statements inside the braces of a loop body are not repeated; they run once, before or after the loop. | right: Every statement inside the loop braces is part of the body and runs on every pass.
wrong: Omits braces around a single-statement body of if, for or while. | right: Braces are optional for a single-statement body, but using them anyway avoids bugs when statements are added later.

Indentation makes the nesting of blocks visible, so the reader can see which statements belong to which block.
A statement block is a sequence of statements, each terminated by a semicolon, enclosed in braces; the body of main() is such a sequence.
